To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the adrenocorticotropic response is activated by hypothalamic aggression and that hypothalamic aggression is facilitated by the adrenocortex, even if the opponent is removed.

(1) the adrenocorticoid response is rapidly activated by hypothalamic stimulation in rats that are not in a fight; and (2) hypothalamic aggression is rapidly facilitated by corticosterone in rats that are adrenalectomized.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fast, positive feedback between a brain mechanism controlling aggressive behavior and the adrenocortex.
the question of how the brain controls aggression and how the stress hormone corticosterone influences the control of aggression.
the question of whether the brain mechanism controlling aggression is influenced by the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-adrenocortical system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stress response is not a cause, but a consequence of aggression, and that the stress response facilitates aggression.
there is a positive feedback between the stress response and aggression, which is mediated through the hypothalamus and the pituitary-adrenal axis.
the hypothalamus is the brain center that controls aggression, and the hypothalamus also controls the adrenocortex, which in turn controls the hypothalamus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the adrenocorticoid stress response and the brain mechanism controlling aggression are closely interrelated.
the hypothalamus is a key structure for the control of aggression and that the adrenocortex and its hormones play a crucial role in this control.
the hypothalamic aggression system has the capacity to rapidly facilitate the stress response, and that the adrenocorticoid stress system, in turn, facilitates hypothalamic aggression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stress response can be activated by a hypothalamic mechanism that controls aggressive behavior.
the brain mechanism involved in aggression can be activated by the adrenocorticoid hormones.
the stress response and aggressive behavior are not independent, but mutually facilitate each other.
